rabato.etymology: F. rabat, fr. rabattre. See Rabate.

rabbet.etymology: F. raboter to plane, plane down,rabot a plane; pref. re- re- + OF. abouter, aboter. See Abut, and cf. Rebut.

rabbi.etymology: L., fr. Gr. "rabbi`, Heb. rabi my master, from rab master, lord, teacher, akin to Ar. rabb.

rabid.etymology: L. rabidus, from rabere to rave. See Rage, n.

raccoon.etymology: F. raton, prop., a little rat, fr. rat rat, perhaps of German origin. See Rat.

race.etymology: OF. raïz, L. radix, -icis. See Radix.

raceme.etymology: L. racemus a bunch of berries, a cluster of grapes. See Raisin.

rack.etymology: AS. hracca neck, hinder part of the head; cf. AS. hraca throat, G. rachen throat, E. retch.

racket.etymology: F. raquette; cf. Sp. raquets, It. racchetta, which is perhaps for retichetta, and fr. L. rete a net (cf. Reticule); or perh. from the Arabic; cf. Ar. raha the palm of the hand (used at first to strike the ball), and OF. rachette, rasquette, carpus, tarsus.

raddle.etymology: Cf. G. räder, rädel, sieve, or perhaps E. reed.

radiant.etymology: L. radians, -antis, p. pr. of radiare to emit rays or beams, fr. radius ray: cf. F. radiant. See Radius, Ray a divergent line.

radiate.etymology: L. radiatus, p. p. of radiare to furnish with spokes or rays, to radiate, fr. radius. See Radius, Ray a divergent line.

radical.etymology: F., fr. L. radicalis having roots, fr. radix, - icis, a root. See Radix.

radicle.etymology: L. radicula, dim. of radix, -icis, root: cf. F. radicule. See Radix.

roots.meaning: A combining form indicating connection with, or relation to, a radius or ray; specifically (Anat.), with the radius of the forearm; as, radio-ulnar, radiomuscular, radiocarpal.
A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.

radiometer.etymology: L. radius radius + -meter: cf. F. radiomètre.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

radish.etymology: F. radis; cf. It. radice, Pr. raditz: all fr. L. radix, -icis, a root, an edible root, especially a radish, akin to E. wort. See Wort, and cf. Eradicate, Race a root, Radix.

radius.etymology: L., a staff, rod, spoke of a wheel, radius, ray. See Ray a divergent line.

raffle.etymology: F. rafle; faire rafle to sweep stakes, fr. rafter to carry or sweep away, rafler tout to sweep stakes; of German origin; cf. G. raffeln to snatch up, to rake. See Raff, v.

raft.etymology: Originally, a rafter, spar, and fr. Icel. raptr a rafter; akin to Dan. raft, Prov. G. raff a rafter, spar; cf. OHG. rafo, ravo, a beam, rafter, Icel. raf roof. Cf. Rafter, n.

rafter.etymology: AS. ræfter; akin to E. raft, n. See Raft.

rag.etymology: Cf. Icel. rægja to calumniate, OHG, ruogen to accuse, G. rügen to censure, AS. wregan, Goth. wrohjan to accuse.

ragamuffin.etymology: Cf. Ragamofin, the name of a demon in some of the old mysteries.

rage.etymology: F., fr. L. rabies, fr. rabere to rave; cf. Skr. rabh to seize, rabhas violence. Cf. Rabid, Rabies, Rave.

ragout.etymology: F. ragoût, fr. ragoûter to restore one's appetite, fr. L. pref. re- re- + ad to + gustare to taste, gustus taste. See Gust relish.

raid.etymology: Icel. reiedh a riding, raid; akin to E. road. See Road a way.

rail.etymology: OE. reil, reýel, AS. hrægel, hrægl a garment; akin to OHG. hregil, OFries. hreil.

raillery.etymology: F. raillerie, fr. railler. See Rail to scoff.

rain.etymology: AS. regnian, akin to G. regnen, Goth. rignjan. See Rain, n.

rainbow.etymology: AS. regenboga, akin to G. regenbogen. See Rain, and Bow anything bent,

raise.etymology: OE. reisen, Icel. reisa, causative of risa to rise. See Rise, and cf. Rear to raise.

raisin.etymology: F. raisin grape, raisin, L. racemus cluster of grapes or berries; cf. Gr. Raceme.

rajah.etymology: Hind. raja, Skr. rajan, akin to L. rex, regis. See Regal, a.

rajpoot.etymology: Hind. raj-put, Skr. raja-putra king's son.

rajput.etymology: Hind. raj-put, Skr. raja-putra king's son.

rake.etymology: AS. race; akin to OD. rake, D. reek, OHG, rehho, G. rechen, Icel, reka a shovel, and to Goth. rikan to heap up, collect, and perhaps to Gr. rack to stretch. Cf. Reckon.

rale.etymology: F. râle. Cf. Rail the bird.

rally.etymology: OF. ralier, F. rallier, fr. L. pref. re- + ad + ligare to bind. See Ra-, and 1st Ally.

ram.etymology: AS. ramm, ram; akin to OHG. & D. ram, Prov. G. ramm, and perh. to Icel. ramr strong.

ramadan.etymology: Ar. ramadan, or ramazan, properly, the hot month.

ramble.etymology: For rammle, fr. Prov. E. rame to roam. Cf. Roam.

rambutan.etymology: Malay rambutan, fr. rambut hair of the head.

ramify.etymology: F. ramifier, LL. ramificare, fr. L. ramus a branch + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See -fy.

ramose.etymology: L. ramosus, from ramus a branch.

ramp.etymology: F. ramper to creep, OF., to climb; of German origin; cf. G. raffen to snatch, LG. & D. rapen. See Rap to snatch, and cf. Romp.

rampant.etymology: F., p. pr. of ramper to creep. See Ramp, v.

rampart.etymology: F. rempart, OF. rempar, fr. remparer to fortify, se remparer to fence or intrench one's self; re- re- pref. + pref. en- (L. in) + parer to defend, parry, prepare, L. parare to prepape. See Pare.

A prefix signifying in or into, used in many English words, chiefly those borrowed from the French. Some English words are written indifferently with en- or in-. For ease of pronunciation it is commonly changed to em- before p, b, and m, as in employ, embody, emmew. It is sometimes used to give a causal force, as in enable, enfeeble, to cause to be, or to make, able, or feeble; and sometimes merely gives an intensive force, as in enchasten. See In-.

rampion.etymology: Cf. F. raiponce, Sp. ruiponce, reponche, L. raperonzo, NL. rapuntium, fr. L. rapum, rapa, a turnip, rape. Cf. Rape a plant.

rancid.etymology: L. rancidus, fr. rancere to be rancid or rank.

rancor.etymology: OE. rancour, OF. rancor, rancur, F. rancune, fr. L. rancor rancidity, rankness; tropically, an old grudge, rancor, fr. rancere to be rank or rancid.

rand.etymology: AS. rand, rond; akin to D., Dan., Sw., & G. rand, Icel. rönd, and probably to E. rind.

random.etymology: OE. randon, OF. randon force, violence, rapidity, a randon, de randon, violently, suddenly, rapidly, prob. of German origin; cf. G. rand edge, border, OHG. rant shield, edge of a shield, akin to E. rand, n. See Rand, n.

range.etymology: OE. rengen, OF. rengier, F. ranger, OF. renc row, rank, F. rang; of German origin. See Rane, n.

rani.etymology: Hind. rani, Skr. rajni. See Rajah.

rank.etymology: AS. ranc strong, proud; cf. D. rank slender, Dan. rank upright, erect, Prov. G. rank slender, Icel. rakkr slender, bold. The meaning seems to have been influenced by L. rancidus, E. rancid.

ransack.etymology: OE. ransaken, Icel, rannsaka to explore, examine; rann a house (akin to Goth. razn house, AS. ræsn plank, beam) + the root of sækja to seek, akin to E. seek. See Seek, and cf. Rest repose.

ransom.etymology: OE. raunson, raunsoun, OF. rançon, raençon, raançon, F. rançon, fr. L. redemptio, fr. redimere to redeem. See Redeem, and cf. Redemption.

rant.etymology: OD. ranten, randen, to dote, to be enraged.

ranula.etymology: L., a little frog, a little swelling on the tongue of cattle, dim. of rana a frog.

ranunculus.etymology: L., a little frog, a medicinal plant, perhaps crowfoot, dim. of rana a frog; cf. raccare to roar.

rapacious.etymology: L. rapax, -acis, from rapere to seize and carry off, to snatch away. See Rapid.

rapacity.etymology: L. rapacitas: cf. F. rapacite. See Rapacious.

rapid.etymology: L. rapidus, fr. rapere to seize and carry off, to snatch or hurry away; perhaps akin to Gr. rapide. Cf. Harpy, Ravish.

rapier.etymology: F. rapière, perhaps for raspière, and ultimately of German origin, akin to E. rasp, v.

rapine.etymology: F. rapine; cf. Pr. & It. rapina; all fr. L. rapina, fr. rapere to seize and carry off by force. See Rapid, and cf. Raven rapine.

rappee.etymology: F. râpé, fr. râper to grate, to rasp. See Rasp, v.

rapport.etymology: F., fr. rapporter to bring again or back, to refer; pref. re- re- + apporter to bring, L. apporter to bring, L. apportare. Cf. Report.

rapt.etymology: From F. rapt abduction, rape, L. raptus, fr. rapere to seize and carry off, to transport; or fr. E. rapt, a. See Rapt, a., and Rapid.

raptor.etymology: L. raptor, from rapere to ravish. See Rapid.

rapture.etymology: L. rapere, raptum, to carry off by force. See Rapid.

rarefy.etymology: F. raréfier; L. rarus rare + -ficare (in comp.) to make; cf. L. rarefacere. See -fy.

rarity.etymology: L. raritas: cf. F. rareté. See Rare.

rascal.etymology: OE. rascaille rabble, probably from an OF. racaille, F. racaille the rabble, rubbish, probably akin to F. racler to scrape, (assumed) LL. rasiculare, rasicare, fr. L. radere, rasum. See Rase, v.

rase.etymology: F. raser, LL. rasare to scrape often, v. freq. fr. L. radere, rasum, to scrape, shave; cf. Skr. rad to scratch, gnaw, L. rodere to gnaw. Cf. Raze, Razee, Razor, Rodent.

rasher.etymology: In sense 1, probably fr. rash, a., as being hastily cooked.

rasp.etymology: OF. rasper, F. râper, to scrape, grate, rasp, fr. OHG. raspon to scrape together, to collect, probably akin to E. rap. Cf. Rap to snatch.

raspberry.etymology: From E. rasp, in allusion to the apparent roughness of the fruit.

rat.etymology: AS. ræt; akin to D. rat, OHG. rato, ratta, G. ratte, ratze, OLG. ratta, LG. & Dan. rotte, Sw. råtta, F. rat, Ir. & Gael radan, Armor. raz, of unknown origin. Cf. Raccoon.

ratafia.etymology: F., fr. Malay arak arrack + tafia a spirit distilled from molasses.

ratchet.etymology: Properly a diminutive from the same word as rack: cf. F. rochet. See 2d Ratch, Rack the instrument.

rate.etymology: Perh. fr. E. rate, v. t., to value at a certain rate, to estimate, but more prob. fr. Sw. rata to find fault, to blame, to despise, to hold cheap; cf. Icel. hrat refuse, hrati rubbish.

ratify.etymology: F. ratifier, fr. L. ratus fixed by calculation, firm, valid + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Rate, n., and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

ratio.etymology: L., fr. reri, ratus, to reckon, believe, think, judge. See Reason.

ratiocinate.etymology: L. ratiocinatus, p. p. of ratiocinari, fr. ratio reason. See Ratio.

ration.etymology: F., fr. L. ratio a reckoning, calculation, relation, reference, LL. ratio ration. See Ratio.

rational.etymology: L. rationalis: cf. F. rationnel. See Ratio, Reason, and cf. Rationale.

rationale.etymology: L. rationalis, neut. rationale. See Rational, a.

ratitae.etymology: NL., fr. L. ratis a raft; cf. L. ratitus marked with the figure of a raft.

rattle.etymology: Akin to D. ratelen, G. rasseln, AS. hrætele a rattle, in hrætelwyrt rattlewort; cf. Gr. Rail a bird.

ravage.etymology: F., fr. (assumed) L. rapagium, rapaticum, fr. rapere to carry off by force, to ravish. See Rapacious, Ravish.

rave.etymology: Prov. E. raves, or rathes, a frame laid on a wagon, for carrying hay, etc.

ravel.etymology: . ravelen, D. rafelen, akin to LG. rebeln, rebbeln, reffeln.

raven.etymology: OF. ravine impetuosity, violence, F. ravine ravine. See Ravine, Rapine.

ravish.etymology: OE. ravissen, F. ravir, fr. L. rapere to snatch or tear away, to ravish. See Rapacious, Rapid, and -ish.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to from adjectives from nouns and from adjectives. It denotes relation, resemblance, similarity, and sometimes has a diminutive force; as, selfish, boyish, brutish; whitish, somewhat white.

raw.etymology: AS. hreáw; akin to D. raauw, LG. rau, G. roh, OHG. ro, Icel. hrar, Dan. raa, Sw. rå, L. crudus, Gr. kre`as flesh, Skr. kravis raw flesh. sq. root18. Cf. Crude, Cruel.

ray.etymology: An aphetic form of array; cf. Beray.

razor.etymology: OE. rasour, OF. rasur, LL. rasor: cf. F. rasoir, LL. rasorium. See Raze, v. t., Rase, v. t.

reach.etymology: OE. rechen, AS. ræcan, ræcean, to extend, stretch out; akin to D. reiken, G. reichen, and possibly to AS. rice powerful, rich, E. rich. sq. root115.

read.etymology: OE. reden, ræden, AS. rædan to read, advice, counsel, fr. ræd advise, counsel, rædan (imperf. reord) to advice, counsel, guess; akin to D. raden to advise, G. raten, rathen, Icel. raedha, Goth. redan (in comp.), and perh. also to Skr. radh to succeed. sq. root116. Cf. Riddle.

ready.etymology: AS. ræde; akin to D. gereed, bereid, G. bereit, Goth. garáids fixed, arranged, and possibly to E. ride, as meaning originally, prepared for riding. Cf. Array, 1st Curry.

real.etymology: Sp., fr. real royal, L. regalis. See Regal, and cf. Ree a coin.

realgar.etymology: F. réalgar, Sp. rejalgar, Ar. rahj al ghar powder of the mine.

reality.etymology: Cf. F. réalité, LL. realitas. See 3d Real. and cf. 2d Realty.

really.etymology: From Middle English really , realy , rialliche , equivalent to real +‎ -ly .

realm.etymology: OE. realme, ream, reaume, OF. reialme, roialme, F. royaume, fr. (assumed) LL. regalimen, from L. regalis royal. See Regal.

realty.etymology: OF. réalté, LL. regalitas, fr. L. regalis. See Regal.

ream.etymology: AS. reám, akin to G. rahm.

reap.etymology: OE. repen, AS. ripan to seize, reap; cf. D. rapen to glean, reap, G. raufen to pluck, Goth. raupjan, or E. ripe.

rear.etymology: OF. riere behind, backward, fr. L. retro. Cf. Arrear.

reason.etymology: OE. resoun, F. raison, fr. L. ratio (akin to Goth. rapj number, account, garapjan to count, G. rede speech, reden to speak), fr. reri, ratus, to reckon, believe, think. Cf. Arraign, Rate, Ratio, Ration.

reasonable.etymology: OE. resonable, F. raisonnable, fr. L. rationabilis. See Reason, n.

reave.etymology: AS. reáfian, from reáf spoil, plunder, clothing, reófan to break (cf. bireófan to deprive of); akin to G. rauben to rob, Icel. raufa to rob, rjufa to break, violate, Goth. biráubon to despoil, L. rumpere to break; cf. Skr. lup to break. sq. root114. Cf. Bereave, Rob, v. t., Robe, Rove, v. t., Rupture.

rebate.etymology: F. rebattre to beat again; pref re- re- + battre to beat, L. batuere to beat, strike. See Abate.

. A prefix from the latin preposition, ex, akin to Gr. 'ex or 'ek signifying out of, out, proceeding from. Hence, in composition, it signifies out of, as, in exhale, exclude; off, from, or out. as in exscind; beyond, as, in excess, exceed, excel; and sometimes has a privative sense of without, as in exalbuminuos, exsanguinous. In some words, it intensifies the meaning; in others, it has little affect on the signification. It becomes ef- before f, as in effuse. The form e- occurs instead of ex- before b, d, g, l, m, n, r, and v, as in ebullient, emanate, enormous, etc. In words from the French it often appears as es-, sometimes as s- or é-; as, escape, scape, élite. Ex-, prefixed to names implying office, station, condition, denotes that the person formerly held the office, or is out of the office or condition now; as, ex-president, ex-governor, ex-mayor, ex-convict. The Greek form 'ex becomes ex in English, as in exarch; 'ek becomes ec, as in eccentric.

rhododendron.etymology: L., fr. Gr. "rodo`dendron, literally, rose tree; "ro`don rose + de`ndron tree. See Rose.

rhomb.etymology: L. rhombus, Gr. wrench: cf. F. rhombe. Cf. Rhombus, Rhumb.

rhubarb.etymology: F. rhubarbe, OF. rubarbe, rheubarbe, reubarbare, reobarbe, LL. rheubarbarum for rheum barbarum, Gr. Rha (the Volga) on whose banks it grew. Originally, therefore, it was the barbarian plant from the Rha. Cf. Barbarous, Rhaponticine.

rhumb.etymology: F. rumb, Sp. rumbo, or Pg. rumbo, rumo, probably fr. Gr. Rhomb.

rhyme.etymology: OE. ryme, rime, AS. rim number; akin to OHG. rim number, succession, series, G. reim rhyme. The modern sense is due to the influence of F. rime, which is of German origin, and originally the same word.

roots.meaning: Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.

rhythm.etymology: First coined in 1557, from Latin rhythmus , from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός ( rhuthmós , “ any measured flow or movement, symmetry , rhythm ” ) , from ῥέω ( rhéō , “ to flow, run, stream, gush ” ) .

riant.etymology: F. riant, p. pr. of rire to laugh, L. ridere.

rib.etymology: AS. rib, ribb; akin to D. rib, G. rippe, OHG. rippa, rippi, Dan. ribbe, Icel. rif, Russ. rebro.

ribald.etymology: OE. ribald, ribaud, F. ribaud, OF. ribald, ribault, LL. ribaldus, of German origin; cf. OHG hripa prostitute. For the ending -ald cf. E. Herald.

ribaldry.etymology: OE. ribaldrie, ribaudrie, OF. ribalderie, ribauderie.

ribbon.etymology: OE. riban, OF. riban, F. ruban, probably of German origin; cf. D. ringband collar, necklace, E. ring circle, and band.

ribes.etymology: NL.; cf. Dan. ribs, and Ar. ribas a plant with an acid juice.

rice.etymology: F. riz (cf. Pr. ris, It. riso), L. oryza, Gr. brizi, akin to Skr. vrihi; or perh. akin to E. rye. Cf. Rye.

rich.etymology: OE. riche, AS. rice rich, powerful; akin to OS. riki, D. rijk, G. reich, OHG. rihhi, Icel. rikr, Sw. rik, Dan. rig, Goth. reiks; from a word meaning, ruler, king, probably borrowed from Celtic, and akin to L. rex, regis, king, regere to guide, rule. sq. root283. See Right, and cf. Derrick, Enrich, Rajah, Riches, Royal.

riches.etymology: OE. richesse, F. richesse, from riche rich, of German origin. See Rich,a.

rick.etymology: OE. reek, rek, AS. hreác a heap; akin to hryce rick, Icel. hraukr.

rickets.etymology: Of uncertain origin; but cf. AS. wrigian to bend, D. wrikken to shake, E. wriggle.

rictus.etymology: L., the aperture of the mouth.

rid.etymology: OE. ridden, redden, AS. hreddan to deliver, liberate; akin to D. & LG. redden, G. retten, Dan. redde, Sw. rädda, and perhaps to Skr. to loosen.

riddle.etymology: OE. ridil, AS. hridder; akin to G. reiter, L. cribrum, and to Gr. rein clean. See Crisis, Certain.

ride.etymology: AS. ridan; akin to LG. riden, D. rijden, G. reiten, OHG. ritan, Icel. riedha, Sw. rida, Dan. ride; cf. L. raeda a carriage, which is from a Celtic word. Cf. Road.

ridge.etymology: OE. rigge the back, AS. hrycg; akin to D. rug, G. rÜcken, OHG. rucki, hrukki, Icel. hryggr, Sw. rugg, Dan. ryg. sq. root16.

ridgeling.etymology: Prov. E. riggilt, riggot, ananimal half castrated, a sheep having only one testicle; cf. Prov. G. rigel, rig, a barrow hog, rigler a cock half castrated.

ridicule.etymology: F. ridicule, L. ridiculum a jest, fr. ridiculus. See Ridiculous.

ridiculous.etymology: L. ridiculosus, ridiculus, fr. ridere to laigh. Cf. Risible.

riding.etymology: For thriding, Icel. pr the third part, fr. pri third, akin to E. third. See Third.

rife.etymology: AS. rif abundant, or Icel. rifr munificent; akin to OD. riff, rijve, abundant.

riffle.etymology: CF. G. riffeln, riefeln, to groove. Cf. Rifle a gun.

riffraff.etymology: OE. rif and raf every particle, OF. rif et raf. CF. Raff, and 1st Rifle.

rifle.etymology: F. rifler to rifle, sweep away; of uncertain origin. CF. Raff.

rift.etymology: Dan. rift, fr. rieve to rend. See Rive.

right.etymology: OE. right, riht, AS. riht; akin to D. regt, OS. & OHG. reht, G. recht, Dan. ret, Sw. rätt, Icel. rëttr, Goth. raíhts, L. rectus, p. p. of regere to guide, rule; cf. Skr. straight, right. sq. root115. Cf. Adroit,Alert, Correct, Dress, Regular, Rector, Recto, Rectum, Regent, Region, Realm, Rich, Riyal, Rule.

righteous.etymology: OE. rightways, rightwise, AS.rightwis; riht right + wis wise, having wisdom, prudent. See Right, a., Wise, a.

rigid.etymology: L. rigidus, fr. rigere to be stiff or numb: cf. F. rigide. Cf. Rigor.

rigidity.etymology: L. rigiditas: cf. F. rigidité. See Rigid.

rigmarole.etymology: For ragman roll. See Ragman's roll.

rigorous.etymology: F. rigoureux, LL. rigorosus. See Rigor.

rill.etymology: Cf. LG. rille a small channel or brook, a furrow, a chamfer, OE. rigol a small brook, F. rigole a trench or furrow for water, W. rhill a row, rhigol a little ditch. sq. root11.

rim.etymology: As. rima, reoma, edge; cf. W. rhim, rhimp, a rim, edge, boundary, termination, Armor, rim. Cf. Rind.

rimose.etymology: L. rimosus, fr. rima a chink: cf. F. rimeux.

rind.etymology: AS. rind bark, crust of bread; akin rinta, G. rinde, and probably to E. rand, rim; cf. Skr. ram to end, rest.

rinderpest.etymology: G., fr. rind, pl. rinder, cattle + pest pest, plague.

ring.etymology: AS. hringan; akin to Icel. hringja, Sw. ringa, Dan. ringe, OD. ringhen, ringkelen. sq. root19.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix having a diminutive force; as in streamlet, armlet.

rink.etymology: Scot. renk, rink, rynk, a course, a race; probably fr. AS. hring a ring. See Ring.

rinse.etymology: OE., fr. OF. rincer, rimser, reinser, raïncier, F. rincer; of uncertain origin.

riot.etymology: OF. riote, of uncertain origin; cf. OD. revot, ravot.

rip.etymology: Cf. Icel. hrip a box or basket; perhaps akin to E. corb. Cf. Ripier.

riparian.etymology: L. riparius, fr. ripa a bank. See River, and cf. Arrive.

ripper.etymology: Cf. Rip a basket, or Riparian.

rise.etymology: AS. risan; akin to OS. risan, D. rijzen, OHG. risan to rise, fall, Icel. risa, Goth. urreisan, G. reise journey. CF. Arise, Raise, Rear, v.

risible.etymology: F., fr. L. risibilis, fr. ridere, risum, to laugh. Cf. Ridiculous.

risk.etymology: F. risque; cf. It. risco, risico, rischio, Pg. risco, Sp. riesgo, and also Sp. risco a steep rock; all probably fr. L. resceare to cut off; pref. re- re- + secare to cut; -- the word having been probably first used among sailors. See Section.

ritual.etymology: L. ritualis, fr. ritus a rite: cf. F. rituel.

rival.etymology: F. rival (cf. It. rivale), L. rivales two neigbors having the same brook in common, rivals, fr. rivalis belonging to a brook, fr. rivus a brook. Cf. Rivulet, Rete.

rive.etymology: Icel. rifa, akin to Sw. rifva to pull asunder, burst, tear, Dan. rive to rake, pluck, tear. Cf. Reef of land, Rifle a gun, Rift, Rivel.

river.etymology: F. rivère a river, LL. riparia river, bank of a river, fr. L. riparius belonging to a bank or shore, fr. ripa a bank or shore; of uncertain origin. Cf. Arrive, Riparian.

rivet.etymology: F., fr. river to rivet; perh. fr. Icel. rifa to fasten together. Cf. Reef part of a sail.

rivulet.etymology: Earlier rivolet, It. rivoletto, a dim. fr. rivolo, L. rivulus, dim. of rivus a brook. CF. Rival, Rite.

roach.etymology: OE. rroche; cf. AS. reohha, D. rog, roch, G. roche, LG. ruche, Dan. rokke ray, Sw. rocka, and E. ray a fish.

road.etymology: AS. rad a riding, that on which one rides or travels, a road, fr. ridan to ride. See Ride, and cf. Raid.

roan.etymology: F. rouan; cf. Sp. roano, ruano, It. rovano, roano.

roar.etymology: OE. roren, raren, AS. rarian; akin to G. röhten, OHG. r. sq. root112.

roast.etymology: OE. rosten, OF. rostir, F. rôtir; of German origin; cf. OHG. rosten, G. rösten, fr. OHG. rost, rosta, gridiron, G. rost; cf. AS. hyrstan to roast.

rob.etymology: F.; cf. Sp. rob, It. rob, robbo, Pg. robe, arrobe, Ar. rubb, robb, Per. rub.

robe.etymology: F., fr. LL. rauba a gown, dress, garment; originally, booty, plunder. See Rob, v. t., and cf. Rubbish.

robin.etymology: Properly a pet name for Robert, originally meaning, famebright; F., fron OHG. Roudperht; ruod (in comp.; akin to AS. hr glory, fame, Goth. hr victorius) + beraht bright. See Bright, Hob a clown.

robinia.etymology: NL. So called after Jean Robin, a French herbalist.

robust.etymology: L. robustus oaken, hard, strong, fr. robur strength, a very hard kind of oak; cf. Skr. rabhas violence: cf. F. robuste.

roc.etymology: Ar. & Per. rokh or rukh. Cf. Rook a castle.

rock.etymology: OE. rocke; akin to D. rok, rokken, G. rocken, OHG. roccho, Dan. rok, Icel. rokkr. Cf. Rocket a firework.

rocket.etymology: F. roquette (cf. Sp. ruqueta, It ruchetta), fr. L. eruca.

rod.etymology: The same word as rood. See Rood.

rodent.etymology: L. rodens, -entis, p. pr. of rodere to gnaw. See Rase, v. t., and cf. Rostrum.

rodomontade.etymology: F., fr. It. rodomontana. See Rodomont, n.

roe.etymology: OE. ro, AS. rah; akin to D. ree, G. reh, Icel. ra, SW. rå.

rogation.etymology: L. rogatio, fr. rogare, rogatum, to ask, beg, supplicate: cf. F. rogation. Cf. Abrogate, Arrogant, Probogue.

rogue.etymology: F. rogue proud, haughty, supercilious; cf. Icel. hr a rook, croaker (cf. Rook a bird), or Armor. rok, rog, proud, arogant.

roil.etymology: Cf. OE. roilen to wander; possibly fr. OF. roeler to roll, equiv. to F. rouler. See Roll, v., and cf. Rile.

roister.etymology: Probably fr. F. rustre boor, a clown, clownish, fr. L. rustucus rustic. See Rustic.

roll.etymology: OF. roeler, roler, F. rouler, LL. rotulare, fr. L. royulus, rotula, a little wheel, dim. of rota wheel; akin to G. rad, and to Skr. ratha car, chariot. Cf. Control, Roll, n., Rotary.

roman.etymology: L. Romanus, fr. Roma Rome: cf. F. romain. Cf. Romaic, Romance, Romantic.

romance.etymology: OE. romance, romant, romaunt, OF. romanz, romans, romant, roman, F. roman, romance, fr. LL. Romanice in the Roman language, in the vulgar tongue, i. e., in the vulgar language which sprang from Latin, the language of the Romans, and hence applied to fictitious compositions written in this vulgar tongue; fr. L. Romanicus Roman, fr. Romanus. See Roman, and cf. Romanic, Romaunt, Romansch, Romanza.

romantic.etymology: F. romantique, fr. OF. romant. See Romance.

romanticism.etymology: CF. It. romanticismo, F. romantisme, romanticisme.

romany.etymology: Gypsy romano, romani, adj., gypsy; cf. rom husband.

romp.etymology: A variant of ramp. See Ramp to leap, Rampallian.

rondo.etymology: It. rondò, fr. F. rondeau. See Rondeau.

rood.etymology: AS. rr, D. roede rod, G. ruthe, rute, OHG. ruota. CF. Rod a measure.

roof.etymology: OE. rof, AS. hr top, roof; akin to D. roef cabin, Icel. hr a shed under which ships are built or kept; cf. OS. hr roof, Goth. hr. Cf. Roost.

rook.etymology: F. roc (cf. Sp. roque), fr. Per. & Ar. rokh, or rukh, the rook or castle at chess, also the bird roc (in this sense pehaps a different word); cf. Hind. rath a war chariot, the castle at chess, Skr. ratha a car, a war car. Cf. Roll.

room.etymology: OE. roum, rum, space, AS. rum; akin to OS., OFries. & Icel. rum, D. ruim, G. raum, OHG. rum, Sw. & Dan. rum, Goth. rums, and to AS. rum, adj., spacious, D. ruim, Icel. rumr, Goth. rums; and prob. to L. rus country (cf. Rural), Zend ravanh wide, free, open, ravan a plain.

roost.etymology: AS. hrost; akin to OD. roest roost, roesten to roost, and probably to E. roof. Cf. Roof.

root.etymology: AS. wrotan; akin to wrot a snout, trunk, D. wroeten to root, G. rüssel snout, trunk, proboscis, Icel. rota to root, and perhaps to L. rodere to gnaw (E. rodent) or to E. root, n.

rope.etymology: AS. rap; akin to D. reep, G. reif ring hoop, Icel. reip rope, Sw. rep, Dan. reb, reeb Goth. skaudaraip latchet.

rorqual.etymology: Norw. rorqualus a whale with folds.

rosary.etymology: LL. rosarium a string of beads, L. rosarium a place planted with roses, rosa a rose: cf. F. rosaire. See Rose.

rose.etymology: AS. rose, L. rosa, probably akin to Gr. vard, OPer. vareda; and perhaps to E. wort: cf. F. rose, from the Latin. Cf. Copperas, Rhododendron.

roseate.etymology: Cf. L. roseus, rosatus, prepared from roses. See Roseal, Rose.

rosemary.etymology: OE. rosmarine, L. rosmarinus; ros dew (cf. Russ. rosa, Lith. rasa, Skr. rasa juice) + marinus marine: cf. F. romarin. In English the word has been changed as if it meant the rose of Mary. See Marine.

roseola.etymology: NL., dim. of L. rosa a rose.

rosette.etymology: F., dim. of rose a rose. Cf. Roset.

rosicrucian.etymology: The name is probably due to a German theologian, Johann Valentin Andreä, who in anonymous pamphlets called himself a knight of the Rose Cross (G. Rosenkreuz), using a seal with a St. Andrew's cross and four roses.)

roster.etymology: Perhaps a corruption of register; or cf. roll.

rostrate.etymology: L. rostratus, fr. rostrum a beak. See Rostrum.

rostrum.etymology: L., beak, ship's beak, fr. rodere, rosum, to gnaw. See Rodent.

rot.etymology: OE. rotien, AS. rotian; akin to D. rotten, Prov. G. rotten, OHG. rozz, G. rösten to steep flax, Icel. rotna to rot, Sw. ruttna, Dan. raadne, Icel. rottin rotten. sq. root117. Cf. Ret, Rotten.

rota.etymology: L. rota wheel. The name is said to allude to the design of the floor of the room in which the court used to sit, which was that of a wheel. See Rotary.

rotary.etymology: L. rota a wheel. See Roll, v., and cf. barouche, Rodomontade, Roué, Round, a., Rowel.

rotate.etymology: L. rotatus, p.p. of rotare to turn round like a wheel, fr. rota wheel. See Rotary, and cf. Roue.

rotatory.etymology: Cf. F. rotatoire. See Rotate, Rotary.

rote.etymology: OE. rote, probably of German origin; cf. MHG. rotte, OHG. rota, hrota, LL. chrotta. Cf. Crowd a kind of violin.

rotifera.etymology: NL., from L. rota ferre to bear.

rotten.etymology: Icel. rotinn; akin to Sw. rutten, Dan. radden. See Rot.

rotund.etymology: L. rotundus. See Round, and cf. Rotunda.

rotunda.etymology: Cf. It. rotonda, F. rotonde; both fr. L. rotundus round. See Rotund, a.

roue.etymology: F., properly p.p. of rouer to break upon the wheel, fr. roue a wheel, L. rota. See Rotate, Rotary.

rouge.etymology: F., fr. L. rubeus red, akin to rubere to be red, ruber red. See Red.

rough.etymology: OE. rou, rou, row, rugh, ruh, AS. r; akin to LG. rug, D. rug, D. ruig, ruw, OHG. r, G. rauh, rauch; cf. Lith. raukas wrinkle, rukti to wrinkle. sq. root 18. Cf. Rug, n.

rouleau.etymology: F., a roll, dim. fr. fr. rôle, formerly also spelt roulle. See Roll.

roulette.etymology: F., properly, a little wheel or ball. See Rouleau, Roll.

roumanian.etymology: From Roumania, the name of the country, Roumanian România, fr. Român Roumanian, L. Romanus Roman.

roundel.etymology: OF. rondel a roundelay, F. rondel, rondeau, a dim. fr. rond; for sense 2, cf. F. rondelle a round, a round shield. See Round, a., and cf. Rondel, Rondelay.

roundelay.etymology: OF. rondelet, dim. of rondel. See Roundel, Roundeau, and cf. Roundlet, Rundlet.

rouse.etymology: Perhaps the same word as rouse to start up, "buckle to."

route.etymology: OE. & F. route, OF. rote, fr. L. rupta (sc. via), fr. ruptus, p.p. of rumpere to break; hence, literally, a broken or beaten way or path. See Rout, and cf. Rut a track.

routine.etymology: F., fr. route a path, way, road. See Route, Roterepetition.

rove.etymology: perhaps fr. or akin to reeve.

rover.etymology: D. roover a robber. See Rove, v. i.

rowdy.etymology: From Rout, or Row a brawl.

rowel.etymology: OF. roele, rouele, properly, a little wheel, F. rouelle collop, slice, LL. rotella a little wheel, dim. of L. rota a wheel. See Roll, and cf. Rota.

rowlock.etymology: For oarlock; AS. *rloc, where the second part is skin to G. loch a hole, E. lock a fastening. See Oar, and Lock.

royal.etymology: OE. roial, riall, real, OF. roial. reial, F. royal, fr. L. regalis, fr. rex, regis, king. See Rich, and cf. regal, real a coin, Rial.

royalty.etymology: OF. roialté, royaulté, F. royauté. See Royal, and cf. Regality.

rub.etymology: Probably of Celtic origin; cf. W. rhwbiaw, gael. rub.

rubbish.etymology: OE. robows, robeux, rubble, originally an Old French plural from an assumed dim. of robe, probably in the sense of trash; cf. It. robaccia trash, roba stuff, goods, wares, robe. Thus, etymologically rubbish is the pl. of rubble. See Robe, and cf. Rubble.

rubble.etymology: From an assumed Old French dim. of robe See Rubbish.

rubefacient.etymology: L. rubefaciens, p.pr. of rubefacere to make red; rubere to be red + facere to make.

rubicelle.etymology: Cf. F. rubacelle, rubicelle, fr. L. rubeus red, reddish.

rubicund.etymology: L. rubicundus, fr. rubere to be red, akin to ruber red. See Red.

rubidium.etymology: NL., fr. L. rubidus red, fr. rubere to be red. So called from two dark red spectroscopic lines by means of which it was discovered in the lepidolite from Rozena, Moravia. See Rubicund.

rubric.etymology: OE. rubriche, OF. rubriche, F. rubrique ( cf. it. rubrica), fr. L. rubrica red earth for coloring, red chalk, the title of a law (because written in red), fr. ruber red. See red.

rubricate.etymology: L. rubricatus p.p. of rubricare to color red. See Rubric, n.

ruby.etymology: F. rubis (cf. Pr. robi), LL. rubinus, robinus, fr. L. rubeus red, reddish, akin to ruber. See Rouge, red.

ruck.etymology: Icel hrukkast to wrinkle, hrukka wrinkle, fold.

rudder.etymology: OE. rother, AS. roedher a paddle; akin to D. roer rudder, oar, G. ruder, OHG. roadar, Sw. roder, ror, Dan. roer, ror. sq. root 8. See Row to propel with an oar, and cf. Rother.

rudiment.etymology: L. rudimentum, fr. rudis unwrought, ignorant, rude: cf. F. rudiment. See Rude.

rue.etymology: F. rue, L. ruta, akin to Gr. r.

ruff.etymology: F. ronfle; cf. It. ronfa, Pg. rufa, rifa.

ruffian.etymology: F. rufien, OF. ruffen, ruffian, pimp. libertine, ake; cf. pr. & Sp. rufian, It. ruffiano; all perhaps of German or Dutch origin; cf. G. raufen to pluck, scuffle, fight, OD. roffen to pander. Cf. Ruffle to grow urbulent.

ruffle.etymology: From Ruff a plaited collar, a drum beat, a tumult: cf. OD. ruyffelen to wrinkle.

rug.etymology: Cf. Sw. rugg entanglend hair, ruggig rugged, shaggy, probably akin to E. rough. See Rough, a.

rugose.etymology: L. rugosus, r. ruga a wrinkle.

ruin.etymology: OE. ruine, F. ruine, fr. L. ruina, fr. ruere, rutum, to fall with violence, to rush or tumble down.

ruinous.etymology: L. ruinosus: cf. F. ruineux. See Ruin.

rule.etymology: OE. reule, riule, OF. riule, reule, F. régle, fr. L. regula a ruler, rule, model, fr. regere, rectum, to lead straight, to direct. See Right, a., and cf. Regular.

rum.etymology: probably shortened from prov. E. rumbullion a great tumult, formerly applied in the island of Barbadoes to an intoxicating liquor.

rumble.etymology: OE. romblen, akin to D. rommeln, G. rumpeln, Dan. rumle; cf. Icel. rumja to roar.

ruminant.etymology: L. ruminans, -antis, p.pr.: cf. F. ruminant. See Ruminate.

ruminate.etymology: L. ruminatus, p.p. of ruminari, ruminare, fr. rumen, -inis, throat, akin to ructare to belch, erugere to belch out, Gr. roccettan.

rummage.etymology: For roomage, fr. room; hence originally, a making room, a packing away closely. See Room.

rummer.etymology: D. roemer, romer, akin to G. römer, Sw. remmare; perhaps properly, Roman.

rumor.etymology: F. rumeur, L. rumor; cf. rumificare, rumitare to rumor, Skr. ru to cry.

rump.etymology: OE. rumpe; akin to D. romp trunk, body, LG. rump, G. rumpf, Dan. rumpe rump, Icel. rumpr, Sw. rumpa rump, tail.

run.etymology: OE. rinnen, rennen (imp. ran, p.p. runnen, ronnen). AS. rinnan to flow (imp. ran, p.p. gerunnen), and iernan, irnan, to run (imp. orn, arn, earn, p.p. urnen); akin to D. runnen, renne, OS. & OHG. rinnan, G. rinnen, rennen, Icel. renna, rinna, Sw. rinna, ränna, Dan. rinde, rende, Goth. rinnan, and perh. to L. oriri to rise, Gr. Origin), or perh. to L. rivus brook (cf. Rival). *11. Cf. Ember, a., Rennet.

runcinate.etymology: L. runcinatus, p.p. of runcinareto plane off, fr. runcina a plane.

rune.etymology: AS. run a rune, a secret, a mystery; akin to Icel. run, OHG. & Goth. runa a secret, secret colloquy, G. & Dan. rune rune, and probably to Gr. 'ereyna^n to search for. Cf. Roun to whisper.

rung.etymology: OE. ronge, AS. hrung, a staff, rod, pole; akin to G. runge a short, thick piece of iron or wood, OD. ronghe a prop, support, Icel. röng a rib in a ship, Goth. Hrugga a staff.

runt.etymology: Scot. runt an old cow. rund a bullock, an ox or Rother, a.

rupee.etymology: Hind.r, fr. Skr. r silver, coined silver or gold, handsome.

rupicola.etymology: NL., fr. L. rupes, gen. rupis, a rock + colere to inhabit.

rupture.etymology: L. ruptura, fr. rumpere, ruptum to break: cf. F. rupture. See Reave, and cf. Rout a defeat.

rural.etymology: F., fr. L.ruralis, fr. rus, ruris, the country. Cf. Room space, Rustic.

ruse.etymology: F., fr. OF. reüser, rehuser, to turn aside, to shuffle, retreat, fr. L. recusare to refuse; pref. re- again + causa cause. See Cause, and cf. Recusant.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying back, against, again, anew; as, recline, to lean back; recall, to call back; recede; remove; reclaim, to call out against; repugn, to fight against; recognition, a knowing again; rejoin, to join again; reiterate, reassure. Combinations containing the prefix re- are readily formed, and are for the most part of obvious signification.

rush.etymology: OE. rusche, rische, resche, AS. risce, akin to LG. rusk, risch, D. & G. rusch; all probably fr. L. ruscum butcher's broom; akin to Goth. raus reed, G. rohr.

rusk.etymology: Sp. rosca de mar sea rusks, a kind of biscuit, rosca properly meaning, a screw, spiral.

russet.etymology: F. rousset, dim. of roux red, L. russus (for rudtus, rudhtus), akin to E. red. See Red, and cf. Roussette.

rust.etymology: AS. rust; akin to D. roest, G. & Sw. rost, Icel. ryth; -- named from its color, and akin to E. red. *113. See Red.

rustic.etymology: L. rusticus, fr. rus, ruris, the country: cf. F. rustique. See Rural.

rusticate.etymology: L. rusticaticus, p. p. of rusticari to rusticate. See Rustic.

rustle.etymology: AS. hristlan to rustle; or cf. Sw. rusta to stir, make a riot, or E. rush, v.

rut.etymology: F. rut, OF. ruit, L. ruditus a roaring, fr. rugire to roar; -sp called from the noise made by deer in rutting time.

ruth.etymology: From Rue, v.: cf. Icel. hryggedh, hrygedh.

ruthenium.etymology: NL. So named from the Ruthenians, a Little Russian people, as coming from Russia, the metal having been found in the Ural mountains.

rutile.etymology: L. rutilus red, inclining to golden yellow.

rye.etymology: OE. rie, reie, AS. ryge; akin to Icel. rugr, Sw. råg, Dan. rug, D. rogge, OHG. rocco, roggo, G. rocken, roggen, Lith. rugei, Russ. roje, and perh. To Gr. 'o`ryza rice. Cf. Rice.
